opus-5.5.text:
I think broader usage is actually one of the most underrated sources of signal we have. When a model is only used by researchers or in a narrow set of benchmarks, you get a very distorted picture of what it's good at and where it breaks. Once real people start using it for coding, writing, math homework, customer support, all kinds of strange long-tail tasks, you suddenly see the true distribution of what people need, and it's always much wider and messier than what you imagined in the lab.

That matters for training in a few ways. First, it tells you where the gaps are. You discover domains where the model is confidently wrong, or where it's fine on simple cases but falls apart once the task gets a bit longer or more ambiguous. That helps you decide where to invest in data, in evaluation, and in reinforcement learning environments, instead of just guessing.

Second, usage helps you design better tasks and rewards. A lot of the progress recently has come from reinforcement learning on verifiable problems like math and code, because there you have a clear signal of right or wrong. The hard question is how to extend that to domains where correctness is fuzzier. Seeing how people actually use the model, what they accept, what they correct, what they come back and retry, gives you intuition about what "good" looks like in those domains, and how you might build environments or verifiers around it.

Third, and maybe most important, it keeps you honest. It's very easy to overfit to benchmarks. Real usage is a constant reality check. If a model's scores go up but people don't feel it's more useful, that's a sign you're optimizing the wrong thing.

Of course, you have to be careful. Usage data isn't automatically good training data. There are privacy considerations, and there's noise and bias in what people ask for. So for me it's less about directly training on everything users do, and more about using broad deployment as a compass: it points you toward the domains and capabilities that really matter, and then you build the right data and training pipelines to go after them.

r001.rationale: The response says broader real-world use reveals the wider range of tasks people need, including coding, writing, math, and long-tail tasks.

r002.rationale: It says usage can guide investment in data and training pipelines, but does not specifically propose synthesizing training data for scenarios discovered through use.

r003.rationale: It discusses building environments or verifiers for fuzzier domains, but does not raise reconstructing the environments in which the observed uses took place.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that broader use creates a feedback loop that you simply cannot design from inside a lab.

When a model is used by a small group, you only see the problems that group cares about. The moment it goes out to many people, you start seeing the long tail. Someone uses it for legal contracts, someone for biology questions, someone for writing in a dialect you never thought to collect data for. Those failures are informative. They tell you where your data distribution is thin, and they tell you which capabilities actually matter to people rather than which ones look impressive on a benchmark.

So the first thing broad use gives you is a map of the gaps. The second thing is signal. Every interaction tells you something, even if you handle it carefully and never train directly on user content. Which prompts get retried, which answers get rejected, where people give up. That shapes how you prioritize the next round of data collection and the next round of evaluation.

And there is a third thing, which I think people underestimate. Broad use changes your definition of a domain. In the lab you think of "code" or "math" as neat categories. Real users mix them. They ask a coding question that is really a product question, or a math question that is really about explaining something to a child. That forces you to build training that crosses boundaries, and models trained that way generalize better than ones trained on clean silos.

So I would say the model's use is not downstream of training. It becomes part of the training process itself, just in a longer loop.

r001.rationale: It says wider use reveals a long tail of applications, with examples such as legal contracts, biology, and dialect writing.

r002.rationale: It says observed usage can guide future data collection, but does not propose synthesizing training data for the discovered scenarios.

r003.rationale: It does not raise reconstructing the environments in which observed uses occurred.

astra-6.text: I think broader use helps us understand where the model’s capabilities are still limited. People bring problems from different domains, and those problems can reveal gaps that we might not notice in our own evaluations. We can then use those insights to guide the next round of training—what data we need, which tasks deserve more attention, and where we need domain experts to help assess quality. But usage alone doesn’t automatically improve the model. The key is turning what we learn from that usage into reliable training signals and checking whether the improvements generalize.

r002.rationale: It mentions using insights to guide needed data, but does not propose synthesizing training data for scenarios found through actual use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think broader use creates a feedback loop. When people apply a model in different domains, they reveal tasks, terminology, and failure cases that our original training data may not cover. That helps us understand where to expand the data and which capabilities need more work.

But usage alone doesn’t automatically improve the model. We need to turn that feedback into high-quality training examples, with appropriate consent and domain expertise, and then evaluate whether the model actually improves. The goal is to learn knowledge that transfers across domains while preserving the details that make each domain different.

r001.rationale: It says people using the model in different domains reveal tasks and failure cases, identifying a broader range of application scenarios.

r002.rationale: It proposes turning feedback from actual use into high-quality training examples for the uncovered tasks and domains.

r003.rationale: It does not raise how to reconstruct the environments in which observed uses occurred.
